title: The next phase of global methane policy
gist: Global methane policy is moving beyond the voluntary Global Methane Pledge toward two harder mechanisms — EU import methane-intensity standards from 2030 and a Barbados-led push for a binding oil-and-gas methane treaty by 2027 — reshaping the terrain for Australian climate diplomacy and fossil-fuel export competitiveness.

themes.theme: Momentum and rationale for methane action

insights.claim: Türkiye, Australia's COP31 partner, gave methane a prominent place in its Action Agenda with a goal of halving growth in global waste by 2035 — the waste sector being the third largest source of anthropogenic methane after agriculture and fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Nikolai Drahos
insights.so_what: COP31 host agenda elevates methane and waste — a signal of where new regulatory pressure and abatement demand will land.

insights.claim: The Global Methane Pledge, launched in 2021 with over 100 countries aiming to cut methane at least 30% between 2020 and 2030, has grown to 159 participating countries.
insights.speaker: Nikolai Drahos
insights.so_what: Broad but voluntary participation is the baseline the harder mechanisms are now trying to surpass.
insights.quote: The number of participating countries has since climbed to 159.
insights.locator: In 2021, over 100 countries plus the EU

insights.claim: Around 40% of methane emissions in the oil and gas sector can be avoided at no net cost, making fossil methane abatement one of the most cost-effective ways to limit near-term warming and reduce the risk of triggering climate tipping points.
insights.speaker: Nikolai Drahos
insights.so_what: No-net-cost abatement of 40% is the economic hook that makes methane regulation politically and commercially tractable.
insights.quote: around 40% of methane emissions can be avoided at no net cost
insights.locator: Abating methane emissions from fossil fuels is also cost effective

insights.claim: Despite the momentum, anthropogenic methane emissions have risen since 2020 and are projected to keep rising through 2050 under current policy settings.
insights.speaker: Nikolai Drahos
insights.so_what: The gap between pledges and rising emissions is why binding mechanisms are gaining traction — a driver of future regulatory tightening.
insights.quote: Anthropogenic methane emissions have increased since 2020 and are projected to keep rising
insights.locator: Yet the world is far from on track

insights.claim: From 2030 the EU will require its fossil-fuel imports to meet methane emissions-intensity standards, using its position as a major importer to drive down methane emissions from suppliers.
insights.speaker: Nikolai Drahos
insights.so_what: EU import-intensity standards turn methane performance into market access — a competitiveness factor for gas and LNG exporters from 2030.
insights.quote: the EU is using its position as a major fossil fuel importer to drive down methane emissions from its suppliers
insights.locator: The first involves building on the EU methane regulations

insights.claim: The EU's 2020 methane strategy envisioned cooperation with major Asian gas importers Japan, South Korea and China, and Japan and South Korea launched a voluntary 2023 program requesting supplier methane data that could pave the way for mandatory rules.
insights.speaker: Nikolai Drahos
insights.so_what: If Asian importers follow the EU toward mandatory rules, methane-intensity becomes a global trade condition, not a regional one.
insights.locator: Other countries could join the EU

insights.claim: Barbados PM Mia Mottley is spearheading a binding global methane agreement starting with oil and gas, calling for a coalition of the willing to begin negotiations in 2027 and mobilising the 74-country Climate Vulnerable Forum she chairs, with France, Tuvalu and Micronesia already signalling support.
insights.speaker: Nikolai Drahos
insights.so_what: A binding oil-and-gas methane treaty push with 2027 negotiations is a concrete regulatory horizon for fossil producers to watch.
insights.quote: calling for a coalition of the willing to begin negotiations in 2027
insights.locator: Another route would be a binding global agreement

insights.claim: Major methane emitters China, Russia and India have not signed the Global Methane Pledge, but China last year extended its headline emissions target to non-CO2 gases including methane for the first time.
insights.speaker: Nikolai Drahos
insights.so_what: China's first inclusion of methane in its headline target is a swing signal for whether binding global action can reach the biggest emitters.
insights.quote: China last year extended its headline emissions target to non-CO2 greenhouse gases, including methane, for the first time

insights.claim: Around 75% of Australia's fossil methane emissions are covered by its Safeguard Mechanism, and the Albanese government has established an expert panel on methane-measurement technologies while the Climate Change Authority reviews further fossil-methane action.
insights.speaker: Nikolai Drahos
insights.so_what: Australia's domestic methane coverage positions it to shape — and be judged by — emerging export methane-intensity competition.
insights.quote: Around 75% of its fossil methane emissions are covered by the Safeguard Mechanism
insights.locator: As a middle power with diplomatic finesse

insights.claim: The author argues domestic methane action can position Australia for a world where methane-emissions intensity plays a role in export competitiveness.
insights.speaker: Nikolai Drahos
insights.so_what: Frames methane performance as a future determinant of fossil-export market share — a strategic lens for Australian LNG/coal exposure.
insights.quote: position Australia for a world where methane emissions intensity plays a role in export competitiveness
insights.locator: Domestic action can help set expectations
